title: Semantic Uncertainty Quantification of Hallucinations in LLMs
one_liner: Use a tensor network to measure when an LLM is confident but wrong, bundling multiple generated answers to spot unreliable ones.
lead: Large language models can fluently generate text that sounds credible but is completely made up (called hallucination). The same prompt produces wildly different answers each time, making it hard to know which ones to trust. This paper measures the model's actual confidence using a quantum physics trick that clusters similar answers together, then flags when a confident cluster is likely wrong.

paras: When you ask an LLM a factual question, it generates text one word at a time, and each word has a probability (how likely the model thinks that word is correct). A beginner assumes high probability means the answer is reliable. But LLMs hallucinate: they confidently produce false information. Worse, asking the same question three times gives three different answers, yet they all have high per-word probabilities.

The naive fix is to look at the average probability of all the words in an answer. But this fails because hallucinated answers often have equally high word-probabilities as correct ones. The model is not confused during generation—it is equally confident when wrong.

callout.html: You get multiple answers with similar high probabilities, but some are hallucinations. How do you know which ones to trust without checking against the real world?

steps.text: Sample the model many times on the same prompt.
Convert words to numeric lists (embeddings) that capture meaning.
Arrange embeddings in a network structure inspired by quantum physics, encoding relationships between answers.
Use the network to cluster answers that mean the same thing, even with different wording.
Calculate entropy within each cluster: tight agreement is low entropy, scattered agreement is high.

paras: Instead of looking at word probabilities one at a time, the paper measures how coherent the model's entire cluster of answers is. It changes the object from individual word scores to measuring how scattered or tight a group of similar answers are.

hidden.name: cluster entropy
paras: The paper measures a new quantity: how spread out or tight the model's answers are when grouped by meaning. When the model generates five answers and they all express the same core fact with different wording, the entropy is low (tight). When the five answers scatter across completely different meanings, entropy is high (scattered).

The paper estimates this by building a tensor network (a graph structure where each node and edge carries numerical weights). The network compares answer embeddings pairwise, measuring how much each answer agrees with others, then sums those agreements to get a cluster entropy score. High entropy in a semantic cluster signals hallucination because the model is internally incoherent.

heat.caption: Darker cells show answers that agree more (tight group). Lighter shows scattered opinions (loose group, hallucination risk).

reads.html: Scatter is how mixed or spread out a group is. If all your friends say the same movie is great, scatter is low. If half love it and half hate it, scatter is high.
The paper accounts for how uncertain the model is when choosing between words in a sequence, and whether that uncertainty clusters semantically (same meaning) or scatters (different meanings).

mechanism.h2: Why measuring cluster coherence catches hallucinations
paras: A hallucinated answer is incoherent: when you generate it multiple times (with randomness), you get slightly different text each time. Correct answers coalesce—the model gravitates toward the same semantic content repeatedly. The network measures this coherence by checking whether many answer embeddings (numeric representations of meaning) cluster tightly.

Hallucinations are internally inconsistent. The model has no stable reason to produce that false answer. So if you group answers by meaning and find a group where word-probabilities are high but the answers scatter (say different things), the model is confident-but-incoherent. A scattered cluster means the model's path to that conclusion is unstable, a sign that it is likely fabricated.

math.words: cluster entropy = negative sum over semantic groups of (probability a group is chosen times log of probability), plus an extra term measuring how scattered the embeddings are within each group
math.equation: H(C) = -sum_g p(g) * log(p(g)) + lambda * mean_distance(embeddings in g)
symbols: total entropy of the semantic clusters
one semantic group or cluster of answers
probability that a randomly sampled answer belongs to cluster g
logarithm of that probability, measuring surprise
weight controlling how much internal scatter matters
average distance between answer embeddings within cluster g

worked.title: Tiny worked example
lines: Five answers to 'When was the moon landing?'
Cluster A (correct): three answers all saying '1969' -> p(A) = 0.6
Cluster B (hallucination): two answers saying '1974' and '1982' -> p(B) = 0.4
Term 2 (scatter): Cluster A embeddings cluster tightly (low mean_distance). Cluster B embeddings are far apart (high mean_distance).
With lambda=0.5: Cluster A adds 0.5 * 0.2 = 0.1. Cluster B adds 0.5 * 0.6 = 0.3.
Total entropy for this answer set: 0.674 + 0.1 + 0.3 = 1.074. High entropy in the minority cluster (B) flags it as unreliable.

math.note: The formula penalizes clusters that are both frequent and internally scattered—a sign that the model is confidently generating incoherent outputs.

charts.title: Baseline method (word probability)
charts.note: Looking at average word probability alone misses many hallucinations because the model is equally confident when wrong.

charts.title: This paper (cluster entropy)
charts.note: Grouping answers semantically and measuring internal consistency catches hallucinations the baseline misses, reducing human confusion.

items.b: Ambiguous questions have legitimate semantic scatter.
items.html: If a question has multiple correct answers (e.g. 'famous scientists'), the model will correctly generate different answers. High entropy looks like hallucination but is not. The method needs a domain-specific baseline for expected entropy.

If the embeddings (numeric representations) do not capture semantic meaning well, the tensor network cannot cluster correctly. With bad embeddings, similar hallucinations fail to cluster and scatter across groups, appearing as multiple low-entropy clusters instead of one scattered high-entropy one.
The method needs dozens of answer samples to compute reliable cluster entropy. For expensive models or real-time applications, repeated sampling is costly and slow.
Calibrate the entropy baseline on a small labeled set (correct vs. hallucinated answers) for your domain, use high-quality embeddings, and budget for multiple samples.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple script that: (1) uses an open-source LLM like LLaMA-2-7B; (2) asks ten factual questions (geography, history, math); (3) samples each question 20 times; (4) computes cluster entropy using a pre-built tensor network; (5) flags high-entropy clusters; (6) compares the model's answers against ground truth to verify that flagged clusters actually contain more hallucinations than unflagged ones.
demo.metric_eq: hallucination_detection_AUROC = area under the curve of (entropy threshold vs. true positive rate / false positive rate)
demo.closing: The demo must show that looking at cluster coherence (how scattered the answers are) catches hallucinations that single word probabilities miss, because a hallucinated answer looks fluent word-by-word but falls apart when you compare it to other attempts at the same question.
